<reason>A wins by focusing the comparison on consent’s additional value within tightly controlled public-interest access, rather than unrestricted surveillance. B establishes serious privacy stakes and plausibly identifies risks from additional access, but repeatedly attacks exported files and unreliable declarations instead of A’s stronger safeguards. A also exposes B’s unsupported dismissal of planning losses as marginal and its mischaracterization of compensation as the principal protection. B’s autonomy argument remains meaningful, but permitting brokers’ nonconsensual internal analysis weakens its categorical objection to equally restricted planner analysis. A answers pressure more directly and provides the cleaner proportionality comparison.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s pressure questions forced B to concede that secure planner access falls under the prohibition, abandoning its initial claim that the exception was unnecessary. A then challenged the decisive comparison: additional credentials need not mean additional copies, and incomplete evacuation models can harm people rather than merely spreadsheets.</best_rebuttal>
